methodology: Weekly October 12 pass: checked fourteen original publication archives or directories and added three articles published October 6–9. Two full public contributor accounts and one public lead interview were read; the subscriber-only remainder was excluded. No older articles were added. One directory follow-up timed out; cached and undated listings do not establish complete coverage. Source claims, estimates and our proposed tests remain distinct. Earlier notes and checks are retained; publication dates, check dates and historical metric windows remain separate. Game snapshots were not refreshed.

articles.title: August 2026’s top new PC & console games, revealed...
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: The accessible news section connects discovery reporting with original developer accounts and platform-documentation changes. It points back to the How Many Dudes? retrospective and flags that creating a third-party Steam event does not guarantee promotion.
articles.evidenceType: Public newsletter preview linking developer reports and platform documentation
articles.actionableLesson: Follow the original evidence behind each campaign claim; record event eligibility separately from promised visibility.
applicationSteps: Keep a dated log of the original developer or platform source.
Check current Steamworks event guidance before committing campaign resources.
articles.limitations: This is a digest of the accessible preview. The post is marked Paid; its subscriber-only remainder was not reviewed. No paid ranking table or sales estimate is reproduced here.
articles.access: Public preview read; paid remainder not reviewed

articles.title: Steam has already generated $15B in gross revenue this year
articles.author: Rhys Elliott
articles.summary: Alinea challenges the idea that a middle revenue rank identifies a mid-budget game. Its analysis of ranks 101–1,000 finds a large catalogue presence, including former blockbusters, so current-year chart position alone is a poor production-budget comparison.
hardData: Alinea estimates that 83% of the 900 games ranked 101–1,000 by 2026 Steam gross revenue launched before 2026.
articles.evidenceType: Commercial analyst estimates; original cohort analysis
articles.actionableLesson: Choose comparables by release age, genre, price and production scale before comparing their current revenue ranks.
applicationSteps: Separate new releases from catalogue games in the comparison set.
Keep lifetime outcomes distinct from current-year estimates.
articles.limitations: Alinea's model is not Valve accounting. The selected revenue band is not a representative sample of all indie releases; chart rank does not establish a game's development budget.
articles.access: Public full article

articles.title: How long is too long to spend on your indie game?
articles.author: Cole
articles.summary: Cole argues for smaller projects using a Steam release-history analysis. The useful methodological question is whether time between a studio's releases measures development time: overlapping projects, ports and different teams can break that assumption.
articles.evidenceType: Practitioner analysis using release intervals as a proxy
articles.actionableLesson: Use actual team schedules and staffing when estimating scope; treat release intervals as a research lead, not a verified production duration.
applicationSteps: Record development start, team changes and overlapping projects where disclosed.
Preserve the article's review-count and release-date filters when discussing its sample.
articles.limitations: The cohort excludes low-review games and first-project durations are unknown. A single observed release does not establish that a developer quit. The article's review-threshold claim is not adopted here as an official Steam rule.
articles.access: Public full article; older article newly added to the library

articles.title: Mandrake - Announce Trailer
articles.author: Derek Lieu
articles.summary: Lieu describes planning Mandrake's reveal before full trailer production: select recognizable life-sim actions, pair them with the game's darker character, and prioritize the footage and art needed to communicate that combination.
articles.evidenceType: First-person trailer-production account
articles.actionableLesson: Plan a reveal around a few playable genre anchors and one distinctive feeling; each narration line should have a clear visual purpose.
applicationSteps: List the familiar actions that identify the genre.
Capture those actions with the game's distinctive tone visible.
Test whether a viewer can describe both the activity and its twist.
articles.limitations: Craft guidance from one selected client project, not controlled evidence that editing caused reach or sales. Publication date follows the visible April 4 byline; the URL contains April 3.
articles.access: Public full article; older article newly added to the library

articles.title: 10 Key Takeaways from IMPACT! Indie Games Pitch Up 2025
articles.author: Ashley Gwinnell
articles.summary: An event recap turns publisher feedback into practical pitch improvements: put the game's identity, working footage, schedule and financial needs early, then make the build easy for different decision-makers to assess.
articles.evidenceType: First-party event notes summarizing publisher-panel feedback
articles.actionableLesson: Prepare a concise fact sheet and short gameplay demonstration that explain the player promise and the concrete support being requested.
applicationSteps: Show actual footage alongside the premise.
State the budget, schedule, current evidence and remaining needs.
Adapt the pitch to the publisher's relevant portfolio.
articles.limitations: Selected panel feedback from 2025, not a universal publisher policy or a measured chance of securing a deal. No acceptance-rate or sales-conversion claim is adopted.
articles.access: Public full article; older article newly added to the library

articles.title: You probably shouldn’t launch a horror game in October
articles.author: Chris Zukowski
articles.summary: Zukowski challenges the rush to finish horror games for Halloween. His monthly release comparison and selected catalogue examples separate the launch decision from later seasonal promotion.
articles.evidenceType: Practitioner analysis of commercial revenue estimates and selected examples
articles.actionableLesson: Choose a launch window around readiness and relevant competition; evaluate seasonal promotion separately.
applicationSteps: Compare similarly scoped releases and retain their release years.
Record launch readiness and later promotional opportunities as separate decisions.
articles.limitations: Unequal release-age windows, a model revenue floor and a revenue-filtered subset limit the month comparison. It does not prove June causes better sales. The author also cautions against moving an already committed October launch because of this post.
articles.access: Public full article text read

articles.title: Does your Steam demo CCU ‘predict’ your game’s success?
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Carless compares demo and full-game peak concurrent players across a filtered release cohort. The distribution makes demo engagement useful for scenario planning while showing why a median cannot forecast an individual launch.
hardData: GameDiscoverCo reports a 3.01× median full-game/demo peak-CCU ratio for 2,569 Steam games released January 2024–August 2026 whose demos exceeded 50 peak concurrents.
articles.evidenceType: Analyst cohort analysis using proprietary Steam concurrency records
articles.actionableLesson: Compare a range of engagement outcomes for similar games before using demo results in a budget.
applicationSteps: Keep the demo threshold, release window and peak-CCU definition with the comparison.
Separate concurrent players from purchases and revenue.
articles.limitations: The selected cohort excludes games without a qualifying demo. All-time peaks have unequal observation windows; pricing, promotion and game quality differ. The ratio is observational, and the article’s sales conversions are estimates.
articles.access: Public full article text read

articles.title: When 1.0 goes nice: Yet Another Zombie Survivors edition
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: The public lead case describes a substantial update and more targeted outreach at Yet Another Zombie Survivors’ exit from Early Access. Returning owners explain why renewed activity must be measured separately from new purchases.
hardData: Awesome Games Studio’s Diana Biszczanik reports 88,000 Steam copies sold in the first two weeks after the August 20, 2026 1.0 launch, compared with 93,000 in Early Access’s first two weeks.
articles.evidenceType: Developer figures reported in an analyst interview; accessible lead section
articles.actionableLesson: Give returning players a clear reason to revisit and explain the new content to relevant creators.
applicationSteps: Measure returning owners, new players and purchases separately.
Show the update’s concrete additions in a focused outreach pitch.
articles.limitations: One successful studio’s self-report does not establish a typical 1.0 result or isolate outreach effects. Paid material after the lead case was not reviewed.
articles.access: Public lead case read; post marked Paid, subscriber-only remainder excluded

articles.title: This year's top PlayStation Plus games (so far)
articles.author: Rhys Elliott
articles.summary: The Steam section distinguishes two demo measures: the share of buyers who tried a demo and the share of demo players who purchased. Those denominators answer different questions.
hardData: As published September 8, Alinea estimates that about 40% of Onimusha’s Steam players previously played its demo, while 25% of demo players bought the Steam game.
articles.evidenceType: Commercial analyst estimates for a selected major-publisher release
articles.actionableLesson: Name the denominator and observation date whenever reporting demo conversion.
applicationSteps: Track demo-to-purchase conversion separately from prior-demo participation among buyers.
Compare matching platforms, regions and acquisition windows.
articles.limitations: These are model estimates for an established franchise, not audited sales or an indie benchmark. The figures do not isolate the demo’s incremental effect, and the exact conversion window is not disclosed.
articles.access: Public full article text read; note covers the Steam demo section

articles.title: Is the game biz sustainable for the average indie dev?
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Carless uses a monthly release cohort to examine how production costs and publishing terms change the revenue needed to sustain a studio. The analysis supplies a useful counterweight to individual breakout stories.
hardData: In its September 15 snapshot, GameDiscoverCo estimates that 16 of 1,230 January 2026 Steam paid releases exceeded $1 million in lifetime gross revenue.
articles.evidenceType: Commercial analyst estimates with illustrative budget and recoup scenarios
articles.actionableLesson: Our interpretation: evaluate a production plan against several net-receipt scenarios and the time between releases.
applicationSteps: Model costs and cash timing separately from gross sales.
Compare releases with similar scope and team circumstances.
articles.limitations: The cohort mixes budgets and experience levels. Cost and recoup assumptions are illustrative; estimated gross and hypothetical net are not audited profit or a particular studio’s success probability.
articles.access: Public full article text read

articles.title: The one ‘game discovery by player age’ chart you need to see
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Carless compares reported discovery habits across age groups in GameDiscoverCo’s Steam Fan Snapshot panel. The practical value is a question for audience research: whether a planned channel matches the players being sought.
hardData: The September 18 article describes a panel of over 16,000 worldwide Steam players recruited through online giveaways; respondents could select multiple discovery methods.
articles.evidenceType: Self-selected survey linked to Steam libraries; self-reported discovery methods
articles.actionableLesson: Our interpretation: test channel fit with the intended audience before allocating campaign effort.
applicationSteps: Ask target players where they found recent games.
Separate reported discovery from tracked visits, wishlists and purchases.
articles.limitations: Giveaway recruitment is not random sampling. Age-group associations do not establish channel effectiveness, acquisition cost or incremental sales. Subgroup sample sizes are not supplied in the accessible text.
articles.access: Public lead analysis read; post marked Paid, subscriber-only remainder excluded

articles.title: Wardogs had a better Steam launch than Helldivers 2 and Arc Raiders
articles.author: Rhys Elliott
articles.summary: Elliott examines Wardogs’ launch through estimated wishlist conversion, acquisition timing and audience overlap. Its pre-order activity makes the distinction between total copies and conversions from the remaining launch wishlist pool especially relevant.
hardData: Alinea’s September 16 article estimates an early-access launch pool of about 1.8 million Steam wishlists and 11% conversion after seven days.
articles.evidenceType: Commercial analyst estimates and observational launch analysis
articles.actionableLesson: Our interpretation: keep pre-orders, launch wishlists and post-launch conversions as separate measures.
applicationSteps: Record the starting pool and conversion window.
Compare acquisition-age cohorts without treating timing as a causal explanation.
articles.limitations: These are Alinea estimates, not Valve or publisher accounts. A selected large shooter launch is not a small-team benchmark; price, community and wishlist recency are not isolated causes of performance.
articles.access: Public full article text read

articles.title: BeamNG.drive - the biggest driving game hit nobody analyzes?
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Carless examines a vehicle sandbox whose community creates different reasons to play and watch. Developer comments connect its continuing audience growth with mods, creator videos and an established simulation technology.
hardData: GameDiscoverCo estimates 1.3 million Steam copies sold in the twelve months preceding its September 22, 2026 article.
articles.evidenceType: Analyst sales estimates and named developer comments
articles.actionableLesson: Our proposal: test whether the same mechanic supports several understandable player-made situations before expanding content production.
applicationSteps: Capture contrasting uses of one mechanic.
Record creator reach separately from attributable purchases.
articles.limitations: A mature technology business is not a short-development benchmark. Estimates are not audited sales; interview explanations do not isolate marketing effects. Mods also create support and rights-management obligations.
articles.access: Public full article; note covers the BeamNG case

articles.title: What are Steam Deck’s biggest 2026 hits - and top genres?
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Carless compares overall handheld popularity with reviews from people who played mostly on Steam Deck. Those measures answer different questions: a large audience and a high handheld share need not identify the same games.
hardData: The September 25 comparison filters for games above $1m gross revenue and 100 Deck reviews; UFO 50 has a 19.2% majority-Deck review share.
articles.evidenceType: Analyst comparison using Steam review play-device indicators
articles.actionableLesson: Our proposal: use relevant handheld comparables to prioritize control and readability tests, then validate the experience on hardware.
applicationSteps: Check controller navigation and small-screen text.
Keep device-specific review share separate from sales forecasts.
articles.limitations: The indicator concerns reviewers with over half their playtime on Deck, not all buyers or revenue. The filtered sample excludes smaller outcomes. Switch performance remains a hypothesis for any new game.
articles.access: Public lead analysis read; post marked Paid, subscriber-only weekly remainder excluded

articles.title: No more universal Daily Deals on Steam - is that good?
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Carless examines planned personalization of Steam discount placements. His analysis suggests exposure may become more frequent and audience-specific, rather than concentrated in a scheduled store-wide promotion.
hardData: The October 2 report places rollout in early 2027; that is a reported plan, not a completed change.
articles.evidenceType: Analyst interpretation of a platform announcement
articles.actionableLesson: Our proposal: compare discount periods using traffic-source reports and net receipts, keeping audience reach separate from purchase conversion.
applicationSteps: Preserve a baseline before the rollout.
Recheck official Steamworks guidance before booking a campaign.
articles.limitations: No game-level revenue gain is established. The linked Valve announcement returned no readable body in this check, so its details remain attributed to Carless.
articles.access: Public lead analysis read; Paid post, subscriber-only weekly remainder excluded

articles.title: What do s&box’s issues (so far) tell us about launching platforms in 2026?
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Carless uses s&box to question whether capable creation tools supply a compelling reason to play. He identifies a gap between a broad platform promise and the experiences its inherited audience expected.
hardData: The September 29 article estimates that 86% of s&box users also own Garry’s Mod; ownership overlap does not measure satisfaction or retention.
articles.evidenceType: Analyst audience estimate and qualitative counter-case
articles.actionableLesson: Our proposal: validate one repeatable player experience before expanding into a creator platform.
applicationSteps: Test the playable hook with people outside the maker community.
Separate creator activity from returning-player activity.
articles.limitations: A well-funded platform is not a small-team cost benchmark. This account cannot isolate why users leave or predict the project’s final outcome.
articles.access: Public full article read; note covers the s&box analysis

articles.title: Q4 games to watch NOT called GTA or Zelda
articles.author: Rhys Elliott
articles.summary: Elliott considers repeat demo use alongside pre-release interest. Guildrun provides an example of checking whether prospective buyers still engage after the initial reveal.
hardData: Alinea’s September 29 estimates: 548k lifetime demo players, 437k wishlists and 6.7 hours median demo playtime.
For September to that point: fewer than 70k new demo players versus more than 150k total active players.
articles.evidenceType: Commercial analyst estimates; pre-release demo cohorts
articles.actionableLesson: Our proposal: track returning demo players separately from first visits and wishlists.
applicationSteps: Compare the same observation windows.
Interview repeat players and early departures separately.
articles.limitations: These are model estimates, not developer telemetry. Activity does not establish paid conversion; subtracting rounded figures would imply false precision. No launch result is claimed.
articles.access: Public full article read; note covers the Guildrun section

articles.title: Steam's top September 2026 games
articles.author: Rhys Elliott
articles.summary: Elliott’s monthly ranking includes older games alongside fresh releases. Bodycam’s update coincides with a strong month, making it a useful dated example for evaluating post-launch investment.
hardData: Alinea estimates Bodycam generated $24.2m on Steam during September 2026, compared with $16m in its Early Access launch month.
The article’s top-500 cohort represents roughly three-quarters of estimated September Steam revenue.
articles.evidenceType: Commercial analyst revenue estimates and selected ranking
articles.actionableLesson: Our proposal: assess an update against development cost, discounts, traffic and returning players before attributing a sales change to content.
applicationSteps: Separate monthly revenue from lifetime totals.
Include weaker comparable updates in the decision sample.
articles.limitations: The ranking omits most releases and cannot establish an indie success rate. Estimated revenue is not studio profit; the update’s causal contribution is unknown.
articles.access: Public full article read; note covers the Bodycam example and sample denominator

articles.title: How Dressmaker became ‘ready to wear’ for hundreds of thousands of players!
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Carless interviews co-creator Jonathan Hau-Yoon about turning sewing expertise into a creative sandbox. The case connects a recognizable activity with customization that players can show to others.
hardData: The October 9 article estimates more than 500,000 Steam units in the first two weeks; these are GameDiscoverCo estimates, not audited sales.
Carless reports a three-person full-time core team and a playable prototype released in July 2025.
articles.evidenceType: Developer interview with commercial analyst estimates
articles.actionableLesson: Our proposal: test whether people understand the activity and want to share their own creations before expanding the feature set.
applicationSteps: Observe unfamiliar players using a small prototype.
Separate recognition of the theme from repeat play and sharing.
articles.limitations: A selected hit does not establish demand for every craft simulator. Publisher history, production costs and channel effects are not controlled; the team count is not a total staffing or budget estimate.
articles.access: Public lead case read; Paid post, subscriber-only weekly remainder excluded

articles.title: How We Took Tiny Eden from 4,800 Wishlists to $700,000 in Its First Two Weeks: A Digital Vortex Publisher Case Study
articles.author: Irina Borodina (guest column); Alexander Semenov (page byline)
articles.summary: Digital Vortex’s CMO describes revising the game, its presentation and campaign before a September launch. The useful distinction is between preparing an audience and receiving a later burst of store traffic.
hardData: The publisher reports over $700,000 revenue during the two weeks after the September 7, 2026 launch; gross/net treatment and costs are unspecified.
The article reports roughly 20,000 Personal Calendar visits versus one million homepage visits during its pre-launch traffic period.
articles.evidenceType: First-person publisher campaign account; unaudited self-report
articles.actionableLesson: Our proposal: record store traffic by placement and date, then assess capsule clarity and purchase behavior separately.
applicationSteps: Keep the campaign timeline alongside product and store-page revisions.
Compare release-date options without assuming a guaranteed homepage slot.
articles.limitations: The author represents the publisher. Concurrent changes prevent causal attribution. Calendar ranking claims are the publisher’s interpretation, not independently verified Valve policy; visit counts do not establish unique people or sales.
articles.access: Public full guest column read

articles.title: Co-dev case study: How Blackbird Interactive and Secret Mode helped Escape the Backrooms ride the Backrooms hype wave
articles.author: Steven Messner
articles.summary: Blackbird Interactive’s communications director describes taking over an established solo project. Recreating its development environment and resolving console matchmaking became prerequisites for the planned ports.
hardData: The account places the handover in September 2025 and the eventual PS5/Xbox release on May 28, 2026, followed by Switch 2 on July 7.
The reported four million players span platforms and a stated month-long period; this is not a Steam paid-unit total.
articles.evidenceType: First-person co-development production account
articles.actionableLesson: Our proposal: test a clean-machine build and real cross-network multiplayer before promising a port date.
applicationSteps: Record engine, plugin and SDK requirements at handover.
Budget separately for platform networking, certification and continued content work.
articles.limitations: The author works for the co-developer. An existing hit, publisher support and a film release limit transfer to a new small-team game. No budget, controlled marketing effect or independently audited player total is supplied.
articles.access: Public full developer-authored article read
